title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio

reading.body:
The core failure here is one of training-data sourcing: an AI music generation system was built using recorded music without the rights holders' authorization. This happened at the model-building stage, before any product reached users, meaning the legal and ethical exposure was embedded in the system from its inception. Catching it would have required rights clearance during data curation, a step that was either skipped or treated as unnecessary.

The reporting describes a disputed legal landscape, not a resolved one. Universal Music Group settled its claims and moved into a licensing partnership, but Sony Music subsequently filed a separate lawsuit alleging the training corpus included over 30,000 of its recordings, and a class action by independent artists was allowed to proceed. Settlements and ongoing litigation are not findings of liability, and the full scope of what was used to train the model has not been established in any court.

What is clear is the structural pattern: a generative model deployed commercially, generating music that competes with the works it may have learned from, with no licensing framework in place at launch. The post-hoc licensing deals now being struck illustrate that the industry is treating authorization as something to negotiate after deployment rather than before it.

summary:
Universal Music Group has reached a settlement with AI music startup Udio, ending a lawsuit that accused the company of using copyrighted songs to train its artificial intelligence system. UMG had claimed that Udio improperly used hits like The Temptations' "My Girl" to create similar melodies without permission or payment. Under the new licensing agreements, Udio will launch a platform next year that uses only authorized and licensed music, allowing users to customize, stream, and share songs created with AI. The financial terms of the settlement were not disclosed.

Udio, founded in 2024 by former Google DeepMind employees, generates original music from text prompts using artificial intelligence. The company said artists can opt into the new platform and will be compensated, though specific details remain unclear. This marks Udio's first music licensing agreement with a major label. UMG also announced a separate partnership with Stability AI to develop music creation tools for artists and producers, as the music industry continues navigating the opportunities and challenges presented by artificial intelligence technology.
